A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MOOSE-Star research. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison. The original theoretical appendix and evaluation rubric are retained, with the rubric moving from Appendix C to Appendix E.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and hypothesis-composition experiments, search comparisons, sampling pass rates, and training and inference scaling results in Tables 1–5 and Figures 2–3.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds frontier-model comparisons, multitask-model results, retrieval ablations, joint retrieval–composition measurements and a reconstruction case study.

M1.justification: Section 6.1 introduces MS-7B, jointly trained on IR and HC data with one copy of bounded-composition data, alongside the retained specialist models. This changes the training procedure for an added variant; the core decomposition, bounded composition, hierarchical search and motivation-planning procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Appendix C adds retrieval scenarios with all-random negatives, all-hard negatives and an irrelevant decoy cluster, changing the candidate environment. TOMATO-Star and its temporal coverage remain unchanged. Newly listing medicine, medical imaging and psychology does not establish additional data collection, and Appendix D reuses the existing temporal discovery setting.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 substantially expand the comparisons by adding GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini-3-Flash, Gemini-3-Pro, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and GPT-5.4. MS-7B also joins the retained specialist-model comparisons, and Appendix D compares several HC backends under a common retriever.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include controlled negative-pool replacements with fixed queries and positives in Appendix C, and joint retrieval–composition success on 200 samples using retrieval cutoffs of 25, 50 and 100 and M3 thresholds of 4–12 in Appendix D. Existing temporal splits and Table 4 search settings remain unchanged. Newly identified judges do not establish replacements of earlier judges.

E4.justification: Appendix C introduces targeted controls testing whether retrieval exploits candidate-cluster shortcuts. Appendix D adds retrieval-versus-composition bottleneck analysis and a complete two-inspiration case study. Table 5 newly breaks HC sampling success down by problem complexity, and Table 3 extends retrieval-noise analysis to the multitask model.

E5.justification: Both versions specify four pairwise evaluations across two independent trials with original and swapped positions in Section 7.3. No new seed reporting, repeated-training-run counts, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures are introduced.

E6.justification: Numerous existing results change: Table 2's MS-HC-7B total moves from 5.08 to 4.68, Table 3's corresponding Hard score from 2.20 to 2.39, Table 5's aggregate HC pass rate from 47.33% to 49.60%, and Figure 3a's brute-force endpoint from 41.3% to 38.5%. Figures also contain revised curves and win distributions. Frontier, multitask and appendix results are added. These are revised reported outcomes; the PDFs do not establish why existing scores changed.

T1.justification: The complexity expressions and decomposition equations are retained. Appendix B preserves the uniqueness, fixed-order, Markov and conditional-independence assumptions, derivation, and permutation-based generalization. Notation refinements and expanded explanations do not introduce new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same central claims: combinatorial intractability of direct training, tractable decomposed training, best-case logarithmic search, scalable inference, and release of 108,717 processed papers. Added experiments support these claims without redefining their main scope.

C2.justification: Section 6.1 adds an explanation distinguishing near-frontier retrieval from composition's greater dependence on base-model reasoning capacity, plus an interpretation of multitask benefits. Appendix C interprets shortcut controls as evidence of content-based retrieval. Appendix D identifies retrieval and composition bottlenecks and explicitly limits its evidence to temporal reconstruction rather than prospective validation.

D1.justification: v2 identifies GPT-4o as the HC evaluation judge and R1-Distilled-Qwen-32B as both generator and scorer for Table 5. It also discloses the approximately 35/65 hard/random negative mixture and the multitask training-data combination. Separate title-page dataset/model links become a collection link; actual resource availability cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 adds the GPT-4o system-card citation and references supporting the new case study. Section 5.4 elaborates how MOOSE-Chem2's hierarchical hypothesis-space optimization motivates inspiration-space search. ResearchBench's venue update refers to the same work, and the broader related-work positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes MOOSE-Star/TOMATO-Star styling, edits local wording and cross-references, expands Section 5.4's explanation and condenses Section 7.1. New appendices precede the relocated rubric, and Appendix A gains a naming explanation. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Tables 1–2 gain substantial frontier-model blocks and grouping labels, Table 5 gains HC rows by complexity, and new Tables 6–8 display ablations, joint success rates and case-study retrievals. Figure 2b has a revised vertical scale, and figures and surrounding text are reflowed. These materially expand the results presentation beyond numerical substitutions.

improvement.justification: The frontier comparisons and targeted shortcut controls strengthen the empirical assessment beyond v1's limited comparator set, while Appendix D makes practical bottlenecks and validation limits clearer. These support a limited net improvement. However, Table 5's new HC passed-sample rows sum to 96,129 rather than the reported 96,879, and the new 12/12 case proposes a TREM2 effect opposite to its accompanying ground-truth passage. These reporting and evaluation problems limit confidence in the expanded evidence.
